cmo-cmo-1987-01.title: Primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$
cmo-cmo-1987-01.body:
**Lemma.** If a prime $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ divides $a^2 + b^2$, then $p \mid a$ and $p \mid b$; hence $p^2 \mid a^2 + b^2$.

*Proof.* If $p \nmid a$, let $a'$ be an inverse of $a$ mod $p$; then $(ba')^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p$. Raising to the power $\frac{p-1}{2}$ (an odd number) and using Fermat, $1 \equiv (ba')^{p-1} \equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/2} = -1 \pmod p$, impossible for $p > 2$. So $p \mid a$, then $p \mid b^2$ and $p \mid b$. $\square$

**Ruling out most $n$.**
* $n = 1$: $a^2 + b^2 = 1$ has no solution in positive integers.
* $n = 3, 4, 5$: $n! = 6, 24, 120$ is divisible by $3$ but not by $9$; by the lemma (with $p = 3$) there is no solution.
* $7 \le n \le 13$: $n!$ is divisible by $7$ but not by $49$ (the only multiple of $7$ up to $13$ is $7$); by the lemma (with $p = 7$) there is no solution.

**$n = 2$:** $a^2 + b^2 = 2$ gives $a = b = 1$.

**$n = 6$:** $a^2 + b^2 = 720$. By the lemma $3 \mid a, b$: $a = 3a_1$, $b = 3b_1$, $a_1^2 + b_1^2 = 80$. Squares are $0$ or $1$ mod $4$, so a sum of two squares divisible by $4$ has both numbers even: $a_1 = 2a_2$, $b_1 = 2b_2$, $a_2^2 + b_2^2 = 20$; again $a_2 = 2c$, $b_2 = 2d$, $c^2 + d^2 = 5$, whose only solution with $1 \le c \le d$ is $c = 1$, $d = 2$. Thus $a = 12$, $b = 24$; check: $144 + 576 = 720$ ✓.

**Answer: $(a, b, n) = (1, 1, 2)$ and $(12, 24, 6)$.** ∎

cmo-cmo-1987-01.title: Computer-style check
cmo-cmo-1987-01.body: For each $n \le 13$ one can test all $a \le \sqrt{n!/2}$ and check whether $n! - a^2$ is a perfect square. This search (easy by computer) finds exactly $1^2 + 1^2 = 2!$ and $12^2 + 24^2 = 6!$, confirming the answer above.

cmo-cmo-1987-02.title: Divisibility by $b - 1$
cmo-cmo-1987-02.body:
We have $1987 = xb^2 + yb + z$ with digits $0 \le x, y, z \le b - 1$, $x \ge 1$, and $x + y + z = 25$. Subtracting,
$$1987 - 25 = x(b^2 - 1) + y(b - 1), \quad\text{so}\quad (b - 1) \mid 1962 = 2\cdot3^2\cdot109.$$
A three-digit representation needs $b^2 \le 1987 < b^3$. Since $12^3 = 1728 < 1987$ and $45^2 = 2025 > 1987$, we get $13 \le b \le 44$, i.e. $12 \le b - 1 \le 43$. The divisors of $1962$ are $1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 109, 218, \dots$, and the only one in $[12, 43]$ is $18$. So $b = 19$.

In base $19$: $1987 = 5\cdot361 + 182$ and $182 = 9\cdot 19 + 11$, so $x = 5$, $y = 9$, $z = 11$, and indeed $5 + 9 + 11 = 25$ ✓.

**Answer: $x = 5$, $y = 9$, $z = 11$, $b = 19$.** ∎

cmo-cmo-1987-03.title: Angle chase and case analysis
cmo-cmo-1987-03.body:
Write all angles in degrees. Let $\alpha = \angle DAB$, $\beta = \angle ABD$, $\gamma = \angle ADB = 180 - \alpha - \beta$, and $\varphi = \angle BED$.

**Angles of the three triangles.** Since $AD \parallel BC$, $\angle DBE = \angle DBC = \angle ADB = \gamma$; since $AB \parallel DC$, $\angle BDC = \angle ABD = \beta$; and $\angle DCE = \angle DCB = \angle DAB = \alpha$. As $E$ lies between $B$ and $C$, $\angle DEC = 180 - \varphi$. So:
* $BAD$: angles $\alpha,\ \beta,\ \gamma$;
* $BED$: angles $\gamma$ (at $B$), $\varphi$ (at $E$), $\psi = 180 - \gamma - \varphi$ (at $D$);
* $DEC$: angles $180 - \varphi$ (at $E$), $\alpha$ (at $C$), $\varphi - \alpha$ (at $D$).

All must be positive: $\alpha, \beta, \gamma > 0$, $\psi > 0$, $\varphi > \alpha$. Conversely, any such $\alpha, \beta, \varphi$ give a valid figure: build triangle $ABD$ and the parallelogram, and draw from $D$ the ray inside $\angle BDC$ making angle $\psi < \beta$ with $DB$; it meets segment $BC$ at an interior point $E$ with $\angle BED = \varphi$.

A triangle is isosceles iff two of its angles are equal. Go through the three possibilities for $DEC$:

**(i) $180 - \varphi = \alpha$**, i.e. $\varphi = 180 - \alpha$; then $\psi = \alpha - \gamma$.
* $\gamma = \varphi$: gives $\beta = 0$. ✗
* $\gamma = \psi$: $\gamma = \alpha/2$, $\beta = 180 - \frac{3\alpha}{2}$. Now $BAD$: $\alpha = \beta$ gives $\alpha = 72$ ✓ ($\beta = 72$, $\gamma = 36$, $\varphi = 108$); $\alpha = \gamma$ is impossible; $\beta = \gamma$ gives $\alpha = 90$, but then $\varphi = 90 = \alpha$. ✗
* $\varphi = \psi$: $\varphi = 90 - \gamma/2$, so $\gamma = 2\alpha - 180 < 0$ (as $\alpha < \varphi$ forces $\alpha < 90$). ✗

**(ii) $180 - \varphi = \varphi - \alpha$**, i.e. $\varphi = 90 + \alpha/2$; then $\psi = 90 - \gamma - \alpha/2$.
* $\gamma = \varphi$: $\psi = -\alpha < 0$. ✗
* $\gamma = \psi$: $\gamma = 45 - \alpha/4$ (then $\psi = \gamma > 0$), $\beta = 135 - \frac{3\alpha}{4}$. $BAD$: $\alpha = \beta$ gives $\alpha = \frac{540}{7}$ ✓; $\alpha = \gamma$ gives $\alpha = 36$ ✓ ($\beta = 108$, $\gamma = 36$, $\varphi = 108$); $\beta = \gamma$ gives $\alpha = 180$. ✗
* $\varphi = \psi$: gives $\gamma = -\alpha$. ✗

**(iii) $\alpha = \varphi - \alpha$**, i.e. $\varphi = 2\alpha$; then $\psi = 180 - \gamma - 2\alpha$.
* $\gamma = \varphi = 2\alpha$: $\psi = 180 - 4\alpha > 0$ needs $\alpha < 45$; $\beta = 180 - 3\alpha$. $BAD$: $\alpha = \beta$ gives $\alpha = 45$ ✗; $\alpha = \gamma$ ✗; $\beta = \gamma$ gives $\alpha = 36$ ✓ ($\beta = 72$, $\gamma = 72$, $\varphi = 72$).
* $\gamma = \psi$: $\gamma = 90 - \alpha$, $\beta = 90$, $\psi = 90 - \alpha > 0$. $BAD$: $\alpha = \beta = 90$ ✗; $\alpha = \gamma$ gives $\alpha = 45$ ✓; $\beta = \gamma$ ✗.
* $\varphi = \psi$: $\gamma = 180 - 4\alpha$ (needs $\alpha < 45$), $\beta = 3\alpha$, $\psi = 2\alpha$. $BAD$: $\alpha = \beta$ ✗; $\alpha = \gamma$ gives $\alpha = 36$ ✓ ($\beta = 108$, $\gamma = 36$, $\varphi = 72$); $\beta = \gamma$ gives $\alpha = \frac{180}{7}$ ✓.

Every case marked ✓ satisfies all positivity conditions, so each gives a genuine figure (e.g. $\alpha = 72$: $AB = BE = ED = DC$ and $AD = BD$, the golden-ratio figure).

**Answer:** $\angle DAB$ can be $\frac{180^\circ}{7},\ 36^\circ,\ 45^\circ,\ 72^\circ$ or $\frac{540^\circ}{7}$. ∎

cmo-cmo-1987-04.title: Induction on the closest pair
cmo-cmo-1987-04.body:
Since each person's distances to the others are all different, each person has a unique nearest neighbour, so the shooting is well defined.

**Odd $n$, by induction.** For $n = 1$ the single person is dry. Let $n \ge 3$ be odd and assume the claim for $n - 2$. Choose two people $A$, $B$ whose distance $AB$ is the smallest of all pairwise distances. Then $AB \le AX$ for every other person $X$, and since $A$'s distances are all different, $AB < AX$: $A$ shoots $B$. Likewise $B$ shoots $A$.

* If some third person also shoots $A$ or $B$, then at least $3$ of the $n$ shots hit $A$ or $B$, so at most $n - 3$ shots hit the remaining $n - 2$ people, and one of them is dry.
* Otherwise nobody besides $A$, $B$ shoots $A$ or $B$. Remove $A$ and $B$. Each of the remaining $n - 2$ people had their nearest person among the remaining ones, so they shoot exactly as before, and the distance condition still holds. By the induction hypothesis ($n - 2$ is odd) one of them is not hit by the others among them — and $A$, $B$ don't hit him either. So he stays dry.

**Even $n$: no.** For $n = 2$ the two people shoot each other and both get wet. More generally, for $n = 4$ put the people on a line at positions $0, 1, 10, 12$: the distances from each person are $\{1, 10, 12\}$, $\{1, 9, 11\}$, $\{10, 9, 2\}$, $\{12, 11, 2\}$ (all distinct), and the shots go $0 \leftrightarrow 1$, $10 \leftrightarrow 12$, so everyone is hit. (Placing $n/2$ such pairs very far apart, with different gaps, works for every even $n$.)

**Answer:** for odd $n$ someone stays dry; for even $n$ this is not always true. ∎

cmo-cmo-1987-05.title: Squeeze and squares mod 4
cmo-cmo-1987-05.body:
**Squeeze.** $(\sqrt n + \sqrt{n+1})^2 = 2n + 1 + 2\sqrt{n(n+1)}$, and
$$n^2 < n(n+1) < n^2 + n + \tfrac14 = \left(n + \tfrac12\right)^2 \implies n < \sqrt{n(n+1)} < n + \tfrac12.$$
Hence $4n + 1 < (\sqrt n + \sqrt{n+1})^2 < 4n + 2$, so
$$\sqrt{4n+1} < \sqrt n + \sqrt{n+1} < \sqrt{4n+2} < \sqrt{4n+3}.$$

**No square in between.** Let $m = [\sqrt{4n+1}]$, so $m^2 \le 4n+1 < (m+1)^2$, i.e. $(m+1)^2 \ge 4n + 2$. Squares are $\equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$, so $(m+1)^2 \ne 4n+2, 4n+3$; therefore $(m+1)^2 \ge 4n + 4 > 4n + 3$. Thus
$$m \le \sqrt{4n+1} < \sqrt n + \sqrt{n+1} < \sqrt{4n+2} < \sqrt{4n+3} < m + 1,$$
and all four numbers have integer part $m$. ∎
